body_markdown:
Once upon a time, 125 years ago, there was a motor vehicle race in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, and the victor used the occasion to secure the financing needed to create his company. That winner was Henry Ford, and the high-profile victory ensured the creation of the Ford Motor Company. But this isn’t a story about the past, as[that moment](https://www.fromtheroad.ford.com/us/en/articles/2026/ford-racing-125-years-winning) became the foundation for Ford’s latest creation: a tribute vehicle called the Ford Racing R125 Mustang.


Built for this year’s SEMA show, the R125 Mustang aims to commemorate Ford’s racing victory in 1901 with a car that is true to the brand’s approachable heritage. The parts chosen ensured this build is intended for lower budgets and daily-driven endeavors, but it doesn’t skimp on the performance you’d expect from Ford Racing’s product portfolio.

The Ford Racing R125 starts with a 1966 Mustang fastback and packs it with a 347-cubic-inch stroker version of Ford’s classic small-block V-8. It utilizes a Boss 302–style block with aluminum heads and is fed by Edelbrock fuel injection.


A pair of two-piece valve covers finishes off the package with a more modern style worthy of Ford’s Coyote V-8. Their patented design includes interchangeable covers, with integrated spark plug wire looms. This treatment hasn’t been seen on a small-block Ford but has been commonplace on the company’s Modular and Coyote V-8 counterparts since the early 1990s.


The valve covers point to Ford Racing’s mission with this commemorative Mustang, as it’s a modest touch that personalizes the small-block V-8 without taking away from its functionality and serviceability. Take a look at the photo below; when was the last time you saw a small-block Ford with a spark plug wiring loom this tidy?


Wes Duenkel


A TREMEC TKX 600 five-speed manual transmission rounds out the powertrain, and it’s beefier than your average gearbox from a donor SN95 Mustang. We’ve seen many Mustang builds with a six-speed manual swap, but this unit retains the compact dimensions that lower budgets demand. Ford suggests this gearbox needs “very minimal floor pan modifications” to fit inside the Mustang’s chassis.


While six forward gears are nice to have, such excess goes beyond the mission of this more humble Mustang restomod. Car-show and showroom cars alike continue to spike in their asking prices, but this nostalgic throwback replicates what makes the Mustang so special: impressive performance with less impact to one’s pocketbook.


Wes Duenkel


And that value proposition has been Ford’s raison d’etre since the first hot rodders got their hands on a Model T. The history of Ford Racing and the Mustang deserve to be celebrated, and the R125 is an honest implementation of what makes the Ford Motor Company so enduring.
